title: ‘I’m not in a hurry’: Trump bats down concerns of Iran war affecting midterms – US politics live
summary: ‘Elections take care of themselves’, says US president when asked if ongoing Iran war could cost Republicans control of Congress
body: Donald Trump switched aircraft before departing Turkey earlier this month after US officials determined there was a credible threat from Iranian proxy forces targeting him and Air Force One, according to a new report from the New York Times. The threat surfaced while the US president was attending the Nato summit. He had arrived in Ankara onboard the new Qatari-donated Boeing 747-8, an aircraft that Trump acknowledged does not have the same advanced defensive systems as the older Air Force One. According to the anonymous sources who spoke to the Times, after US officials detected the threat, the Secret Service recommended that Trump change aircraft before leaving the country. He later announced he would depart on the older Air Force One instead. The newly reported details about the threat help explain why the White House quickly decided to swap aircraft. They also highlight ongoing security concerns surrounding the donated jet, which Trump had pushed to have ready for use as soon as possible. According to the report, US officials did not believe the Iranian proxy forces were specifically targeting the new Boeing 747-8. Instead, the intelligence indicated the threat was directed at Trump himself and whichever aircraft he was traveling on. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, Donald Trump repeated his claim that Israel would not exist today had he lost the 2004 presidential election to Kamala Harris. Asked about his comment on Thursday that he was “considering a massive attack” on Iran, Trump renewed his threat and said: “if I thought they were anywhere near getting a nuclear weapon- if I wasn’t elected, Israel would, in my opinion, not be around any more. They would have been hit by a nuclear weapon”. The president went to on to claim, as he has previously, that “Barack Hussein Obama’s nuclear deal” with Iran, “was a road to a nuclear weapon”. That claim is contradicted by the preamble to the 2015 agreement, which said, “Iran reaffirms that under no circumstances will Iran ever seek, develop or acquire any nuclear weapons”, and by the mechanism spelled out in the deal for rigorous international inspections Iran agreed to as a condition of the agreement. Trump then claimed that only his order to bomb nuclear sites in Iran in 2025 had prevented that nation from building nuclear weapons and using them to destroy Israel. “If that didn’t happen, they would have a nuclear weapon and there would be no Israel,” Trump said. “If they had a nuclear weapon, they would have used that. There might not be a Middle East as we know it today.” Trump’s claim that Iran was about to build nuclear weapons is contradicted by the 2025 US intelligence assessment presented to Congress by his own director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, before the strikes he ordered, which clearly stated that the collective assessment of 18 US intelligence agencies was “that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and Supreme Leader Khamanei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003.” Trump’s claim that Iran would have used nuclear weapons to destroy Israel also clashes with the logic of deterrence, specifically the doctrine known as mutually assured destruction, since Iran is aware that Israel already has nuclear weapons it could use to destroy Iran. The fact that Israel’s Jewish population is intertwined with a Palestinian population of similar size across a very small geographical area also makes it hard to see how the Jewish state could be destroyed in a nuclear attack that did not also kill vast numbers of Palestinians, and lay waste to Islam’s third holiest site, Jerusalem’s al-Aqsa Mosque. Still, Trump’s comments do echo claims his partner in the war on Iran, Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has made for decades, and repeated in last month at a policy summit in Jerusalem. “We have prevented Iran from carrying out a plan to annihilate us, and today they would have had a nuclear weapon, an atomic bomb to do so,” Netanyahu said. “We removed an existential danger. And had we not acted … Iran would have had atomic bombs. And let me tell you something, they would have used them.” Asked by a Fox News correspondent in the Oval Office on Friday where he stands on the question of whether LeBron James or Michael Jordan is the greatest ever basketball player, Donald Trump chose to answer an entirely different question: which NBA great likes him better? “Well, Michael Jordan’s a gut that’s a friend of mine,” Trump began, turning the subject to himself. “I play golf with him; he’s a really good guy. And I think LeBron is- maybe he’s a racist. But maybe he doesn’t like Trump, I don’t know,” the president continued, clearly still irked by LeBron James having called him a “bum” nine years ago, in a social media post after Trump cancelled a White House visit by that year’s NBA champions, the Golden State Warriors, because their star guard, Steph Curry, said he would not go. “Going to White House was a great honor until you showed up!” James posted at the time. “I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way,” Trump said. Asked at the time why he did not want to go to the Trump White House, Curry said the message was: “That we don’t stand for basically what our president has- the things that he’s said and the things that he hasn’t said at the right times, that we won’t stand for it.” “By acting and not going, hopefully that will inspire some change when it comes to what we tolerate in this country, what is accepted and what we turn a blind eye toward,” he added. Donald Trump batted down concerns that the ongoing Iran war – which has seen 13 days of consecutive strikes – could cost Republicans control of Congress in the upcoming midterms. “Despite what everybody says about the election I’m not in a hurry,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We have to do it right. Elections take care of themselves.” In response to the Trump’s vow to inflict “major military punishment” for Tehran, the president said that the White House continues to speak with Iran. “I think they’re getting more and more serious as the days go by,” Trump said. “We can take that to a much higher level if we want to. You know, we’re prepared to do that, as you know. We’re locked and loaded … we’ll see what comes of it.” Notably, Trump declined to answer when New York Times reporter Shawn McCreesh asked whether threats to bomb bridges and other civilian infrastructure in Iran would amount to war crimes. At the White House today, Donald Trump announced that the US now has three nuclear reactors which have reached “criticality” –the state where the reactor’s chain reaction sustains itself without additional input. Later, when asked about the new condition he placed on the US-Saudi Arabia nuclear deal that requires the kingdom to join the Abraham Accords, the president said “it’s a two-way street, and we think it’s very important for the future of the Middle East”. Two US small businesses have sued the Trump administration over its latest round of tariffs, affecting more than 80 countries and aimed at targeting countries that engage in forced labor. According to the lawsuit filed in the US court of international trade by Liberty Justice Center – the same organization that challenged Trump’s tariffs that the top court struck down – the plaintiffs argue that Trump’s latest round of duties require more ‌detailed ⁠country-specific findings about “forced labor” to be legally justified. Meanwhile, Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with “substantial” tariffs after Brussels imposed a series of steep fines on US tech companies. In a post on his Truth Social, the president wrote: “The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!” It comes days after Google was fined €890m ($1bn) by the EU after its search and app store services were found to have breached online competition laws. Trump also said that in recent meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, both leaders assured the US president separately that they would not sell weapons to Iran. The president added: “Two major countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them – certainly not in their best interests.” Later today, Trump ⁠will address the White House Correspondents’ Association at a rescheduled dinner later today, nearly three months after a shooting at the Washington Hilton hotel interrupted the event. The replanned dinner on Friday will only have around 700 guests, compared to the roughly 2,600 that attended in April, and will have enhanced security according to the Secret Service. More here. On Saturday, Maine Democrats will hold a special convention to select a nominee to replace Graham Platner for the US Senate race in November. Troy Jackson – a logger, longtime legislator and former president of the Maine senate – is now poised to clinch the nomination. Last weekend, all of Jackson’s serious challengers in the breakneck race to find a nominee dropped out, clearing a swift and unobstructed path for him. These, in effect, replace the blanket 10% tariff that Trump imposed in February, right after the supreme court declared many of his earlier tariffs were illegal. title: More than 200,000 people flee or lock down as wildfires sweep France and Spain
summary: ‘Highly unpredictable’ blaze forces evacuation of Cap Ferret on French coast and Spain declares national emergency
body: More than 200,000 people have fled or been ordered to lock down as huge wildfires swept Spain and France on Friday, prompting Madrid to declare a national emergency and the French authorities to order the total evacuation, by land and sea, of one of the country’s best-known holiday spots. Authorities in south-west France ordered the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast to be evacuated “village by village” in the face of an “intense, highly unpredictable” wildfire that has burned through more than 19,000 hectares (47,000 acres) of forest. Spain’s government declared its first national emergency for a wildfire as two large blazes merged into one outside Madrid and a third was on the verge of joining them, amid searing heat and tinder-dry conditions across much of southern Europe. Both countries sought EU help. “This is the worst wildfire in our region’s history,” said Madrid’s regional leader, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, describing “an unprecedented situation: a perfect storm of extremely high temperatures and relentless winds”. More than 110,000 people had been evacuated in two days to escape the Cap Ferret fire, the Gironde prefecture said, including thousands of holidaymakers in campsites and rental homes. Boats ferried hundreds off piers on the peninsula on Friday as the blaze threatened to cut off the only access road. Scientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events, evaporating soils and waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading to thousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate. About 800 firefighters and four water-bombing planes were battling the Gironde blaze north of Arcachon Bay, but the fire, which began on Wednesday near the village of Saumos 25 miles (40km) west of Bordeaux, was not yet stabilised. Numerous roads in the area, including those leading to Cap Ferret, which contains many villas owned by celebrities and millionaires, were closed to all but essential traffic. Eighty houses had burned. “I’ve seen plenty of fires before, but never one of this intensity,” Jean Mazodier, 86, who owns 150 hectares of forest and was evacuated from his home at 6am, told Le Monde. “Everything’s burned. It’s like losing a child.” A second fire raging in the region, farther south near the popular holiday resort of Biscarrosse, had also burned through more than 2,500 hectares, the Landes prefect, Gilles Clavreul, said on Friday, and led to the evacuation of about 31,000 people. More than 600 firefighters were struggling to contain that blaze, Clavreul said.“There are a great many new fire starts ahead of the main blaze. The situation is highly dynamic and unfavourable,” he added. In 2022, a wildfire burned more than 30,000 hectares in France’s south-west, forcing 50,000 evacuations. In parched conditions and fanned by strong winds, the two latest blazes have torn through coastal pine forests with flames up to 10 metres (30ft) high. France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had activated the EU’s civil protection mechanism as the country, which has endured three almost back-to-back heatwaves since May, battled numerous wildfires. “We will soon be able to count ‌on reinforcements from two Croatian aircraft, two Portuguese planes, as well as two heavy helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia,” Macron said. France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Friday that 32 wildfires were burning, with 50,000 hectares scorched already so far this year – nearly four times the total by the same date last year. About 800 firefighters were battling a blaze in the south-eastern Var area, where weather conditions were improving, Nuñez said, allowing some firefighting resources to be redeployed to the south-west. The severity of fires in the EU has broken records for the time of year, data from the European Forest Fire Information System shows. Spain’s government declared a national emergency on Thursday evening after wildfires ⁠threatened areas near the capital and in the neighbouring province of Ávila, leading to the evacuation or confinement of more than 63,000 people. A national emergency, which allows central government to assume overall control of powers and responsibilities that are usually the domain of Spain’s self-governing regions, has only been declared once before, during the countrywide blackout of April 2025. The regional government of Madrid requested assistance, describing the situation as one of “extreme gravity”. It said at least four active fires could advance “beyond current extinguishing capacity”. The fires remained uncontained on Friday. Spanish authorities said on Friday afternoon there was “very little time left” before the blaze in Madrid, already made up of two merged fires, combined with the Ávila fire. On Friday night, Madrid’s regional environment minister, Carlos Novillo, said the fire had reached “a critical moment” and was “beyond our extinguishing capability”. He added: “The priority at the moment is protecting people, helping those who have been evacuated, and making the most of windows of opportunity.” José Cobos, who fled his home about 30 miles south-west of Madrid on Friday morning with his wife and three dogs, told Antena 3 television: “The smoke was incredibly thick. You couldn’t breathe.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, chaired an emergency response meeting at the Moncloa palace on Friday morning as the state meteorological office warned that the danger of more fires remained very high. He said the government had deployed “all available resources”, adding: “It will be by your side during the emergency and the recovery.” The prime minister also thanked “all the emergency services that are fighting day and night”. Sánchez is due to visit the affected area on Saturday morning. On Friday morning, Spain’s environment ministry said 29 big forest fires had been recorded so far in 2026, compared with an annual average of nine between January and the end of July per year over the past decade. Forest fires had burned about 114,796 hectares, compared with 25,133 by the same time last year. Spain’s interior ministry has also requested fire-fighting aircraft through the EU’s civil protection mechanism, which aims to strengthen civil protection cooperation between EU countries and 10 additional participating states. Spain’s Guardia Civil force, which polices rural areas, said late on Friday that one man had been arrested and another was under investigation in connection with the forest fire in the Burgohondo municipality of Ávila. It said the two suspects had apparently ignored a ban on the use of heavy machinery, thereby creating “sparks … that may have caused the fire”.

title: Judge rules FDA restrictions on mifepristone are arbitrary and capricious
summary: Abortion medication ruled to be safe as judge orders Trump administration to consider overturning restrictions
body: A federal judge upheld the safety of the abortion medication mifepristone and ordered the Trump administration to examine and consider overturning restrictions on the drug as barriers to abortion access mount across the country. Robert S Ballou, a US district judge in Virginia, ordered the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) on Friday to reconsider mifepristone restrictions, which the judge found to be arbitrary and capricious. Previous FDA reviews have “steadfastly found” that mifepristone is safe and effective, Ballou wrote in his decision. Fifth circuit judges are set to hear arguments in a separate case, with Louisiana asking the FDA to reinstate previous restrictions that would block mail-order mifepristone and put limits on pharmacy prescriptions. The FDA, which currently has no permanent commissioner, says it is conducting a review of abortion pill regulations that has been pushed by conservative lawmakers and activists. The case, Whole Woman’s Health Alliance v FDA, was filed in May 2023 by the Center for Reproductive Rights, representing abortion providers in Virginia, Kansas and Montana. “The efforts to restrict it are not about science or safety – they are about making abortion harder to access,” said Nancy Northup, president and CEO at the center, in a statement. She called Friday’s ruling “a win for science”. The court’s findings are consistent with decades of scientific and clinical studies in this country and internationally, said Joanne Rosen, director of Center for Law and the Public’s Health at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “This decision, however, will not settle the pitched debate over the safety of mifepristone and the conditions under which it should be available, and will be far from the last word,” Rosen said. Several states, including Louisiana, are currently challenging the safety and availability of mifepristone in courts across the country and seeking to have it removed from the market nationwide, or to restrict its access, despite that long record of safety, she added. “So, stay tuned.” The plaintiffs asked the court to remove three medically unnecessary restrictions, including a requirement for providers and pharmacies that prescribe and dispense mifepristone to have a special registration and certification, and for patients to sign “duplicative, inaccurate, and confusing” paperwork, Linda Goldstein, senior counsel at the center, said in the statement. “I have worked in abortion care for over 30 years, and I can attest that these regulations serve no medical purpose, nor do they add value to our patients’ experience of abortion,” said Amy Hagstrom Miller, president and CEO of Whole Woman’s Health Alliance. The “red tape” kept her clinic from seeing patients – the number of whom has increased as patients have been forced to leave their homes in states with bans to seek care elsewhere, she said. “In Kansas, we’ve become a vital access point for people forced to travel long distances for abortion care,”said Kathryn Boyd, president and CEO of Trust Women. “Every barrier lifted would mean fewer delays, less stress and more dignity for our patients.” Abortion pills now account for nearly two-thirds of all abortions in the US, and a quarter-century of studies have indicated the safety and effectiveness of mifepristone.

title: Trump switched planes in Turkey earlier this month because of threat from Iran proxy forces – report
summary: President flew to Ankara onboard Qatari-gifted jet, without advanced defenses, and flew home on old Air Force One
body: Donald Trump switched aircraft before departing Turkey earlier this month after US officials determined there was a credible threat from Iranian proxy forces targeting him and Air Force One, according to a new report from the New York Times. The threat surfaced while the US president was attending the Nato summit. He had arrived in Ankara onboard the new Qatari-donated Boeing 747-8, an aircraft that Trump acknowledged does not have the same advanced defensive systems as the older Air Force One. According to the anonymous sources who spoke to the Times, after US officials detected the threat, the Secret Service recommended that Trump change aircraft before leaving the country. He later announced he would depart on the older Air Force One instead. The newly reported details about the threat help explain why the White House quickly decided to swap aircraft. They also highlight ongoing security concerns surrounding the donated jet, which Trump had pushed to have ready for use as soon as possible. According to the report, US officials did not believe the Iranian proxy forces were specifically targeting the new Boeing 747-8. Instead, the intelligence indicated the threat was directed at Trump himself and whichever aircraft he was traveling on. The White House has been contacted for comment. Trump’s justice department had previously subpoenaed reporters at the New York Times over their coverage of the security risks involving the president’s Qatari-gifted Air Force One replacement, but the justice department has dropped, for now, those efforts. Earlier this month, it was reported that Trump flew part of the trip home from the Nato summit in Turkey aboard the older Air Force One after arriving on the new Qatari-gifted aircraft. At the time, Trump did not provide a detailed explanation for the switch, saying he would use the legacy aircraft “for old time’s sake”. He also said both planes would make a previously unscheduled stop at Royal Air Force Mildenhall, a base used by US troops, before returning to the US. Although Trump did not explain the reason for changing planes at the time, he has previously spoken about threats from Iran against his life, even going so far as to say he left standing orders for the US military to destroy Iran “at levels they’ve never seen before” if Tehran carries out its longstanding threats to kill him. The revelations also come as Trump reportedly mulls escalating attacks on Iran in the ongoing conflict after a ceasefire deal has recently broken down. ⁠Trump has vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, though he once again left open the door to a diplomatic deal with Iran. “We are talking to ⁠them. I think they’re being serious. I think … they are being by far the most serious that we’ve seen them, but that doesn’t mean we get there,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday. He added: “We’re locked and loaded. We’re ready to go.”

title: Two small American businesses sue Trump administration over new tariffs
summary: Lawsuit alleges president’s actions exceed authority of forced labour statue under which levies are being enacted
body: Two small American businesses sued the Trump administration over its new round of sweeping tariffs, launching a fresh legal challenge against Donald Trump’s signature economic policy. The lawsuit was filed by the Liberty Justice Center, which won a US supreme court case against the president’s tariffs earlier this year, forcing the administration to unravel many of its controversial import duties. Trump has aggressively sought alternative pathways to make his trade policy permanent without congressional approval, despite the court’s 6-3 ruling that the president overstepped his executive powers by issuing his “liberation day” tariffs. The latest tariffs, which were announced late on Thursday, will hit more than 80 countries with either a 10% or 12.5% levy. They were implemented under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, which allows the president to bypass congressional approval in order to prevent goods made with “forced labor” from being imported. Trump used this law in his first term to enact tariffs against China, which withstood several court challenges. The plaintiffs of the latest lawsuit argued that Trump’s actions exceed the authority of Section 301, which should be “targeted, country-specific and practice-specific remedial authority”, unlike the vast duties Trump levied on Thursday night. They also allege the US trade representative (USTR) “failed to provide a reasoned, record-based explanation for its determinations” and argued that more country-specific findings about forced labor are needed in order for the tariffs to be legally justified. The USTR did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The two businesses pursuing the lawsuit are Burlap and Barrel, a spice importer based in New York, and Collective Horology, a watchmaker based in California. Both businesses source material from many of the countries hit by tariffs: Burlap and Barrel imports spices from Canada, India, Spain, Turkey and Vietnam, while Collective Horology distributes watches from countries made in the United Kingdom, France and Austria. “These tariffs would punish a responsible American business, and the farmers we work with, without showing how taxes on our spices would address the policies of foreign governments that USTR says it is targeting,” the co-founder and co-CEO of Burlap and Barrel, Ethan Frisch, said in a statement. The Liberty Justice Center is a libertarian public interest law firm that is part of the litigation arm of the Illinois Policy Institute, a free market thinktank. In the case against Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs, the firm argued that Trump relied on emergency powers in order to push his tariffs through. This time around the Liberty Justice Center has argued that Trump is unfairly using the issue of forced labor, echoing the claims that several lawmakers have made since the new tariffs were unveiled. “Forced labor is morally indefensible, but an important objective does not give the government permission to ignore the law,” said Sara Albrecht, CEO of the Liberty Justice Center. “The administration allowed one global tariff to expire and immediately replaced it with another under a different statute. “Changing the statute doesn’t change the law. Every tariff authority has limits, and every administration must respect them.”

title: Trump administration admits canceling clean energy grants to Democratic states
summary: Court fillings show grants denied to states if they didn’t back Trump’s re-election, but administration claims it’s a ‘misrepresentation’
body: The Trump administration has admitted scrapping more than $7.5bn in federal grants for clean energy projects to states “based solely” on whether they backed Donald Trump in the 2024 election. US federal officials appeared to acknowledge in court documents last week that they had terminated the funding last October “based solely” on political criteria, targeting projects in states that were represented by Democrats and had voted for Kamala Harris. The administration previously framed the move as safeguarding taxpayer dollars from “waste” and continues to insist it was not politically motivated. “[The Department of Energy] accepts that neither the inclusion of the ARCHES grant nor any other grants in the October notice tranche was based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor,” government lawyers said in the filing. “[The Department of Energy] accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, ie, whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State. “[The Department of Energy] will not contend that it looked beyond the prime grantee(s) to consider the political identity or geographic distribution of downstream beneficiaries of the grant funds.” The apparent admission was first reported by the New York Times. In a statement on Friday, a spokesperson for the US energy department said of the report: “That is a misrepresentation of the court filing. None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations.” The acknowledgment of political considerations “was referring to the timing of the announcement, not of the decisions themselves”, the spokesperson claimed. The filings stem from a lawsuit, filed last June, by a group of six University of California faculty and other researchers challenging various federal agencies that halted Biden-era funding. The plaintiffs said in a press release at the time that the abrupt cancellations of already-awarded grants had been a part of a “political ‘cost-cutting’ agenda and ideological purity campaign” waged by the administration. It comes as the White House seeks to exert even greater control over billions of dollars in annual federal grants, aiming to have Trump’s political appointees review all federal grants, with the power to block or revoke vast amounts of funding if they did not conform to or align with Trump’s priorities. According to a 400-page proposed rule for federal financial assistance published on 29 May, “Discretionary awards must, where applicable, demonstrably advance the President’s policy priorities.” They must also adhere to further standards set out by the White House, including not promoting “anti-American values”, the denial of “the sex binary in humans” and the use of “racial preferences” in selection criterion. Per last week’s court filing, the energy department had reviewed its financial assistance awards and created a list last September that recommended canceling more than 600 grants awarded by the Biden administration for a wide range of clean energy projects in states represented by both Republicans and Democrats. However, in October, the White House budget office, led by Russell Vought, terminated only 284 of those grants. Vought announced on X: “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being canceled. The projects are in the following states: CA, CO, CT, DE, HI, IL, MD, MA, MN, NH, NJ, NM, NY, OR, VT, WA.” Last week, federal officials appeared to concede that the decision had been purely informed by politics. “With one exception, the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators (“Blue State” grants),” the court filing says. Meanwhile, the energy department left in place hundreds of other energy grants in state represented by Republicans and that had voted for Trump in 2024 – despite the department having also recommended that they too be scrapped. Last month, Trump’s energy secretary, Chris Wright, appeared before the House science, space and technology committee to defend his department’s fiscal 2027 budget request. “No decisions were made on politics,” he insisted. The Guardian has reached out to the White House.

title: Trump threatens EU with ‘substantial’ tariffs over fines of US tech giants
summary: After Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Europe was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayers
body: Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with additional and “substantial” tariffs after Brussels imposed a series of steep fines on US tech giants. The US president accused Brussels of taking “direct aim” at several American companies including Apple, Meta Platforms, Amazon and Google, writing in a Truth Social post: “The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!” Days earlier, Google was fined €890m ($1bn) by the EU after its search and app store services were found to have breached online competition laws. Last year Apple and Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, were also fined. Trump claimed in his social media post on Friday that the US would “immediately” launch an investigation into the EU’s practice of “‘ROBBING’ American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer,” and said that the EU will “pay a very big price” for its actions. It came just a day after the Trump administration separately imposed a sweeping round of tariffs on more than 80 countries, including those in the EU. The European Commission did not immediately comment on Trump’s threat on Friday. Announcing the fine on Google on Wednesday, it said the tech company had given “preferential treatment to its own services, including shopping, hotels, transport and sports results”. Google welcomed Trump’s intervention on Friday. Jose Castaneda, a spokesperson for the company, said Google had worked hard to comply with the EU’s Digital Markets Act and expressed its concerns about the effects of recent decisions by the European Commission. “We appreciate the engagement by the administration and U.S. government,” he said. Trump has often used tariffs – or simply the threat of them – as a way to retaliate against countries for decisions outside trade policy. Last year, he threatened a tax on imports from Mexico and Canada until the two countries agreed to implement measures on border security. Despite challenges from the supreme court, Trump has persisted in implementing tariffs globally, claiming that they will help boost US jobs and manufacturing. The tariffs he announced yesterday would impose a 10% levy on the EU, and were designed to clamp down on what Trump claimed were unfair labor practices. The EU has cracked down on a handful of large tech companies since before the start of Trump’s presidency after passing the Digital Markets Act, meant to help regulate competition among digital media companies.

title: This desert oasis is a biological wonderland. Trump’s border wall threatens to destroy it
summary: Environmental groups are sounding the alarm over plans that threaten a desert spring that’s home to rare fish and turtles and sacred to the O’odham people
body: Quitobaquito Springs in south-west Arizona has been called a biological wonderland with few equals. The springs are an oasis in the vast Sonoran desert along the US-Mexico border, held sacred by the O’odham people, who call it A’al Vaipia. Here, water flows out of an aquifer at the bottom of a hill, runs along a short concrete channel and collects in a pond. The pond is home to Sonoyta pupfish, which are small and silvery, with upturned jaws. In the channel are found small mollusks the size of chia seeds known as springsnails. This is the only place on Earth where these two species live in the wild. It’s also the only US habitat for the Sonoyta mud turtle, a reptile with a domed shell and the ability to survive amid scarce desert water sources. The spring, located within Organ Pipe Cactus national monument, provides one of the only reliable bodies of water for about 100 miles in any direction, making it vital for wildlife in the area and for humans who have lived here for millennia. But the spring is in trouble. In 2020, the Trump administration completed a 30ft-tall (9 meter) border wall in this remote area, during which time the spring flow dipped to an all-time low, and the pond partially dried up after its lining cracked. Now, plans are under way to build a second massive section of the wall, just 90-150 feet north of the existing one. That’s despite border crossings in the area being negligible – the vast majority of people who cross into the country in such remote areas intend to be apprehended so they can apply for asylum, immigration experts report. The planned secondary wall will be made of steel beams, or bollards, also 30ft tall. Similarly designed stretches of secondary or primary fencing are currently under construction at about six other locations on the Arizona-Sonora border, according to Erick Meza, borderlands coordinator with the Sierra Club. “I’ve never seen something of this magnitude,” Meza said. “It’s unbelievable.” Researchers, environmentalists and Indigenous leaders warn the project will cause untold damage to this fragile, remote wilderness and the animals that call it home. The southern edge of the pond lies 190ft from the border with Sonora, meaning part of the pond would probably be destroyed by heavy machinery necessary for putting up the barrier. Even closer to the line is a grove of mesquite trees, which is part of the federally recognized critical habitat for the mud turtle, where the animals often burrow. That would probably be leveled by construction. Putting up a second wall in this place could be catastrophic, said Tara Harris, director of conservation and science at the Phoenix Zoo, who fears the planned construction “could destroy the last remaining habitat for multiple imperiled species”. Illegal immigration in the area of Organ Pipe has been minimal since 2025, according to local residents. In 2023 and 2024, tens of thousands of immigrants seeking asylum came through the wall into Organ Pipe, showing that this barrier doesn’t stop determined people. But those numbers dwindled to almost nothing after the Biden administration sharply limited asylum-seeking. Already, 34 miles (54km) of secondary barriers have been completed along the US-Mexico border, much of that in Arizona, creating a line of two 30ft walls right next to each other. Another 390 miles of these barriers are under construction, and 155 miles have been awarded contracts, including the stretch in Organ Pipe Cactus, according to the Department of Homeland Security’s Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agency. This kind of construction would normally require extensive consultations and studies to adhere to laws including the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act. But the 2005 Real ID Act gives the head of the Department of Homeland Security the authority to waive these and many other laws. The specialness of A’al Vaipia cannot be overstated, said Wynona Larson Yazzie, an O’odham elder and community organizer: it has been a home, gathering place and sacred site for water and ceremonies since time immemorial. The plans to build these barriers throughout the area were “sickening”, she said. A race to save rare turtles and fish The DHS awarded a contract in late May to a company called Sundt Construction to build the new wall section in Organ Pipe Cactus, according to the agency, and work could begin at any moment. Locals have observed contractors surveying the area and setting up flagging and other signs the construction may begin soon. Now, researchers are urgently making plans to save the area’s wildlife. Michael Bogan, an aquatic ecologist with the University of Arizona, leads the recovery team for the Sonoyta mud turtle, and is collaborating with researchers including Harris. Right now, the team is evaluating every option, including the most dire, in which as many of the animals as possible would be taken out, and housed in artificial habitats. The pond is home to about 250 turtles, he said. The only current backup population for the turtle lives at the Arizona-Sonoran Desert Museum, which has 20 of the turtles, said Tom Weaver, the herpetology curator. Their institution is being asked to take up to 50 turtles if need be, which the organization said they were willing to do, despite the enormous work involved. The Phoenix Zoo said they would also take turtles. The organization currently has a population of Quitobaquito springsnails housed in two tanks – the species’ only backup population. The size of their only wild habitat, at the spring, “could fit into the area of three parking spaces. So they’re just incredibly vulnerable,” Harris said. As for the pupfish, there are about five captive backup groups, including in a pond by a learning center in Tucson. While animals can be held temporarily, researchers emphasized that this is not a long-term solution. “Our main concern is that there’s a place for them to go back to,” said Debra Colodner, director of conservation science at the Arizona-Sonoran Desert Museum. The area has already suffered damage from the first wall’s construction in 2020. The existing barrier has cut off important wildlife corridors, where animals from jaguars to black bears to deer pass between the US and Mexico. During the 2020 construction, the bottom of the pond cracked and much of it dried up. The pond had to be relined, during which time some of the aquatic wildlife were temporarily moved by researchers, including Bogan. The flow of the springs also declined to the lowest measure on record. Many blame the digging, heavy traffic and water pumping and worry the impacts this time will be much worse, Bogan said. Contractors use huge quantities of groundwater to create cement for the base of the wall. CBP previously estimated that a single mile of fencing built nearby in 2008 used 710,000 gallons of water; the current project might use more since the new structures are larger. The aquifer that feeds the springs is probably fed both by extremely old groundwater and water from the Rio Sonoyta to the south, according to a thesis by hydrologist Hector Zamora. So groundwater pumping nearby could deplete the aquifer, and if the water table declines to a level below where water exits the spring, it will run dry. “That’s the concern that keeps me up,” Bogan said. John Mennell, a spokesperson for CBP, said in a brief statement that the agency was “working with the US Fish and Wildlife Service and National Park Service to avoid Quitobaquito Springs and minimize impacts to sensitive resources”. But CBP declined to respond to any follow-up questions. When asked about the environmental concerns, Sundt Construction and the National Park Service, which runs the monument, both referred questions to CBP. CBP said they would not pump within five miles of the springs; they said the same in 2020. But there is no data to suggest that this will be enough to protect it, and indeed, a significant portion of the water probably comes from farther away than that, according to Zamora. Aaron Cooper, executive director of the International Sonoran Desert Alliance, a non-profit group that works to protect the cultural resources and ecology of the borderlands, said that CBP had provided almost no information about what it was planning, even as workers had been seen on the border seeming to make preparations for the work. “I have never seen anything with so little planning and oversight, of this scale and scope,” Cooper said. “No outreach, no messaging, no comment periods, absolutely nothing. Radio silence.” ‘Reckless behavior could destroy that place’ Beyond the environmental concerns, many fear more damage to a sacred and historically important Indigenous site. As recently as the 1950s, the area was home to members of the Hia-Ced O’odham, a subset of the larger O’odham community, who were pushed out when the land was purchased by the National Park Service. The springs have always served as a way station on the traditional O’odham route to the Sea of Cortez, where people go to gather salt, according to Christina Bell Andrews, a Hia-Ced O’odham leader and the director of the Wassaja Center for Native American Health at the University of Arizona. Andrews said that building a second wall there would destroy much of the on-site cemetery, and desecrate more than 40 gravesites. In April, Larson Yazzie was leading a group of O’odham people on a prayer run along the border. The group spent the night at the springs, and headed west. A couple of days later, they witnessed a bulldozer clearing land in a protected area, a sacred earthwork known as an intaglia, which is 200ft long, 1,000 years old and shaped like a fish, pointing south toward the sea. They soon realized that contractors had destroyed a big chunk of the intaglia. “Some people took that as a sign of what could happen at Quitobaquito. Such reckless behavior could destroy that place,” sa…

title: Doctor details condition of Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s body in D4vd hearing
summary: Grant Ho, who performed postmortem examination, said he identified two stab wounds on 14-year-old’s body
body: The autopsy of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez’s body took center stage on Friday as a hearing continued to determine whether musician D4vd will stand trial for murder charges linked to her death. Prosecutors say the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, fatally stabbed Hernandez last April to silence her from divulging the sexual nature of their relationship as his career soared. He was 18 and she was 13 when the sexual abuse began, according to prosecutors. Burke has pleaded not guilty to charges including capital murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains. Last September, Los Angeles police discovered Rivas Hernandez’s remains in the front trunk of a Tesla, registered to Burke, five months after prosecutors allege Burke killed her. The court has seen graphic photographs of Rivas Hernandez’s dismembered and decomposing body this week. The degraded conditions of her remains posed challenges to the autopsy, Grant Ho, the doctor who performed the postmortem examination, testified on Friday. Rivas Hernandez had been dead for weeks when her body was found, but Ho noted it was “extremely difficult to tell” when exactly she died. In April, Rivas Hernandez’s autopsy report was unsealed amid mounting scrutiny and speculation over the circumstances of her death. According to the Los Angeles county medical examiner’s office, she died from multiple penetrating injuries. On Friday, Ho said he had identified two stab wounds – one on her abdomen that struck her liver and another on her left chest that damaged her ribs. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Georgia school shooter handed victims’ families ‘life sentence of trauma’, court hears
summary: Colt Gray, who was 14 at time of attack on Apalachee high school, admits 55 charges including four counts of murder
body: The wife of a teacher killed in a high school shooting in Georgia two years ago told a court on Friday that the families of the four victims had been handed “a life sentence of grief and trauma” by the teenage student who murdered them. Shayna Aspinwall, whose husband Richard died at Apalachee high school, about 45 miles north-east Atlanta, on 4 September 2024, was speaking at the sentencing hearing for Colt Gray, 16, who earlier pleaded to 55 charges, including second-degree murder. Gray admitted during a state court hearing in Barrow county superior court in Winder, Georgia, that he carried out the attack, his “non-negotiated” plea deal with prosecutors negating to need for a trial scheduled for October. The agreement meant no sentence was agreed, and instead superior court judge Nicholas Primm heard a summary of the case and evidence from the defense and prosecution before determining the punishment for Gray’s conviction on 55 counts, including second-degree murder. Teachers Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53, were killed in the shooting, as well as students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14. Another teacher and eight other students were wounded, seven of them by gunshots. Shayna Aspinwall told the court that the lives of their daughters, who were two and five when their father died, will be “forever marked by his absence”. “It is a life sentence of grief and trauma for those left behind,” she said. Breanna Schermerhorn, whose son Mason was killed, said she did not forgive Colt Gray. While adults around him missed warning signs, she said, he decided to bring the gun and to pull the trigger. “Those decisions were his and his alone,” she said. “Mason deserved a future and we all deserved a future with Mason in it, and Colt took that from Mason and everyone who loved him.” Gray’s father, Colin Gray, was convicted in March on charges including second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter, and is scheduled to be sentenced next week. Prosecutors said he gave his son the assault-style rifle that was used in the school attack. Colt Gray was led into court for Friday’s hearing with his feet chained together, watched by several relatives of victims in the public gallery. The judge questioned Gray to ensure he understood the consequences of his plea and was entering it voluntarily. Gray responded, “Yes, your honor,” each time. Murder carries a minimum sentence of life in prison. The judge must decide whether Gray should be eligible for parole after hearing victim statements, evidence and each side’s summary of the case. Several family members of those killed, and students who were shot, gave statements expressing anger and grief. Most asked the judge to sentence Gray to life without parole. A teenage student who was wounded, a minor whose identity the Guardian is withholding, recalled the day of the shooting, saying she remembered feeling “really scared and confused because I saw Colt standing in the door with a gun”. She said she realized she had been shot and asked a friend to hold her hand. She asked other friends to call her brother to let him know she had been shot and didn’t know if she would make it. She had multiple surgeries and was unable to walk for about a year. “After the shooting, I struggled with so much anxiety, and I felt like my life was over,” she said. Apalachee high school’s principal, Jessica Rehberg, said Colt Gray’s “cruel actions” deserve “the harshest consequences”. Among the 55 charges were four murder counts and 25 of aggravated assault. Gray, 14 at the time of the shooting, was charged as an adult. According to detectives from the Georgia bureau of investigation, Gray carried the rifle on to the school bus with the barrel wrapped in a poster board, then left his second-period class and emerged from a bathroom with the rifle, shooting people in a classroom and hallway. They said Gray planned the attack carefully, and left instructions and a diagram in a notebook that indicated he believed he could kill as many as 26 people and wound 13 others. Investigators said they found a shrine in Gray’s bedroom to Nikolas Cruz, who murdered 18 people at Florida’s Marjory Stoneman Douglas high school in 2018. Cruz was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2022. Sheriff’s deputies interviewed Colt and Colin Gray in May 2023, 14 months before the attack, about an online threat linked to the son. Colt Gray denied making the threat. Records show he skipped eighth grade, then enrolled as a freshman at Apalachee after the academic year had begun, but did not attend regularly. During Colin Gray’s trial an investigator testified that he was aware his son’s mental health had declined, and had considered, but not arranged, counseling for him. The hearing is expected to extend into next week. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Democrats move to keep South Carolina as first state to vote in 2028 presidential primaries
summary: DNC move aims to better represent views of party’s racially diverse voter base ahead of next presidential cycle
body: Democrats moved to keep South Carolina as the first state to vote in their party’s 2028 presidential primary process, while moving up several other states, in an effort to better represent the views of the party’s racially diverse voter base. At a meeting in Washington DC of the Democratic National Committee’s (DNC) rules and bylaws committee on Friday, South Carolina received a slim majority of votes to take the first spot, scheduled for 22 January 2028, with Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia set to follow, in that order. The selections must still be confirmed by the full DNC at a meeting set for next month. Minyon Moore and James Roosevelt Jr, who co-chair the committee, called the proposal “a rigorous, fair, and efficient calendar that will win Democrats back the White House in 2028”. South Carolina was the state whose primary voters revitalized Joe Biden’s presidential campaign in 2020, and as president he returned the favor by encouraging the DNC to make the state the first to vote in the 2024 nominating calendar. That supplanted New Hampshire, the site for decades of the first primary for both parties, as well as Iowa, which holds caucuses that have traditionally been the first nominating contest of presidential election years. However, both states are overwhelmingly white, and with Democrats increasingly relying on Black, Latino and other minority voters to elect their candidates, the party has sought to move states with larger populations of those groups towards the front of the nominating calendar, where they can play a crucial role in selecting the presidential frontrunners. Making the case for South Carolina, the long-serving congressman James Clyburn said in a statement ahead of the meeting: “We have a record that all of us can point to and be proud of. It’s a relatively small state. It has four distinct cultures, a relatively cheap media market, and demographics that reflect what our voter population needs to be in order for our candidates to be successful in the general election.” During the meeting, the Nevada Democratic chair, Daniele Monroe-Moreno, argued that her state offers the ideal racial mix and nodded to Donald Trump’s success there in 2024, when he became the first Republican in two decades to win its electoral votes. “When we go into the next presidential cycle, my state, the state of Nevada, is that coalition that we need to win back,” she said. The new early voting states are either presidential battlegrounds or home to hotly contested US Senate races and House districts. They also have substantially more Black and Latino voters than the states that led the 2020 nominating calendar, as well as larger populations of voters in unions or without college degrees, both constituencies with which many Democratic candidates have struggled to win in recent elections.

title: Police say alcohol withdrawal caused woman’s death in California backcountry
summary: Joanna Ruth Shields’ body was found in a pool of water with suspicious marks, driving speculation she was attacked
body: A young woman whose body was found in the backcountry of California’s Big Sur with suspicious marks on her face and neck died of alcohol withdrawal, the Monterey county sheriff’s office said on Thursday. The discovery of Joanna Ruth Shields’ body in April had driven widespread suspicion that she had been the victim of a violent attack. A group of hikers found Shields, 37, naked in a pool of water in the Sykes hot springs area of the Ventana wilderness with marks on her neck and a cut across her forehead. The group of hikers also came across a man who reportedly told the group he had been hiking with Shields, and said she had gone to the bathroom without returning. He went looking for her and saw her facedown in a pool of water. The man cooperated with the investigation, the Monterey county sheriff’s office said. The Monterey county sheriff’s office investigated the case as a “suspicious death”. But the findings of Tina Nieto, the sheriff-coroner of Monterey county, ruled the cause of death as “probable alcohol withdrawal seizures due to chronic alcohol use disorder”. The marks on Shields’ neck were the result of insect bites, and the gash on her forehead was “superficial” and did not contribute to her death, according to the Monterey county sheriff’s office. “Our thoughts and prayers remain with Joanna’s family and loved ones,” Nieto wrote in a statement. “We hope these findings provide them with some measure of peace and closure after several difficult months.” Investigators found no evidence during the forensic examination or throughout the investigation to indicate that Shields was the victim of a crime. Shields was a passionate skater who worked as a brand ambassador for Evolve Skateboards.

title: If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world
summary: Forced labor is a problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at all
body: Don’t believe the Trump administration’s rationale for its new volley of tariffs against everybody. The new levies, ostensibly to punish countries for failing to do enough to curb forced labor, switched on at 12.01am on Friday, to coincide with the expiration of a temporary 10% blanket duty that Donald Trump imposed in February, ostensibly to protect the United States from a balance-of-payments crisis. That duty was imposed right after the supreme court struck down tariffs the president unleashed on US trading partners last year on the also spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies. The shifting justifications alone underscore how Trump’s arguments are bullshit. But the specific nature of the latest accusation truly takes the cake. The US is arguing that tariffs of 10% or 12.5% are justified against 60 trading partners because they import stuff made with forced labor, unfairly undercutting American producers. But the charge omits that forced labor is not only prevalent across the US. It is also actively enforced by the state. Americans import lots of stuff made with forced labor: $170bn worth of imported goods are at risk of being tainted at some stage along the supply chain, according to the Global Slavery Index (GSI), from raw materials through to finished products. In 2023, this was the most among the countries in the G20. It includes electronics imported from China and Malaysia; clothing from India, Vietnam and Bangladesh; fish from Ghana; and timber from Russia, Brazil and Peru. The mining of essential minerals used in many electronics the US buys from abroad, from cobalt and copper to lithium and nickel, is rife with allegations of human rights abuses. To be sure, until recently the US was the only country that explicitly prohibited importing goods made with forced, convict or indentured labor. Still, the GSI reports no evidence that penalties are enforced against companies that fail to comply with reporting mandates, due diligence or other procurement regulations. Then there’s the issue of forced labor at home. There were 1.1 million people living in modern slavery in the US on any given day in 2021, according to the GSI, mostly doing domestic work, or toiling in agriculture, construction, retail, hospitality and illicit activities. That amounts to 3.3 forced workers for every thousand people in the population, which is more than in many of the countries Trump wants to punish. In the Netherlands and Germany, there are 0.6 forced workers per thousand people. In Britain there are 1.8. Canada also has a law on the books prohibiting imports made with forced labor. The prevalence of slave labor in Canada is only 1.8 per thousand people. Still, it just got hit with a 10% tariff because according to the US trade representative it is not doing enough to enforce the law. (The European Union will ban imports that involve forced labor starting in 2027.) But here is the real rub: a significant share of modern slavery in the US is enforced by the state. The US stands out among the world’s democracies by allowing forced labor in prisons. And there is no legal obstacle to export goods made by prisoners forced to work against their will. The 13th amendment to the constitution bans slavery and involuntary servitude, but it exempts work “as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted”. In Alabama prisons, they call the forced labor “mandatory chores”. About 800,000 of the 1.2 million people in state and federal prisons work, according to a report in 2022 by the American Civil Liberties Union and the University of Chicago – often against their will, under the threat of further punishment. Incarcerated workers, the report adds, “are under the complete control of their employers, and they have been stripped of even the most minimal protections against labor exploitation and abuse”. Most work for the prisons themselves and other government businesses. In Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and Texas, more than 10,000 prisoners are assigned to agricultural work on penal plantations or prison farms, according to the ACLU report. They are also often farmed out to the private sector. In Alabama, according to an investigation by the Associated Press, they were leased out to at least 500 private businesses between 2018 and mid-March 2024. Prisoners toil in poultry processing plants and work in the kitchens of some of the biggest fast-food chains. They cook, wash dishes, fix plumbing and clean buildings. They are paid pennies an hour. And their wages are often garnished by the state. In seven southern states – Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas – almost all work by prisoners remains unpaid. If he is so inclined, Trump could help the fight against slave labor by taking a hard line against the US’s southern states, which generally raise less tax revenue and thus rely more on “free” work by the incarcerated to both operate prisons and generate revenue for the public sector. The ACLU report estimated that the incarcerated produce stuff worth more than $2bn a year and provide $9bn worth of services to their prisons. Other countries could help by slapping some tariffs on American goods to retaliate against these blatantly unfair practices.

title: US expands Iran attacks as Trump warns Tehran and Houthis over Red Sea strikes
summary: No end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
body: The US has struck targets across Iran, reaching as far as the Caspian Sea, as Donald Trump threatened “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the war to a second shipping ⁠chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea. As Iran retaliated on Friday with missile and drone fire against US bases and allies across the region, the New York Times reported that Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire proposal delivered by the Iraq prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi. This despite the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claiming a day earlier that Iran was begging for a ceasefire. Iraq later disputed the report. Trump warned China and Russia on Friday against selling weapons to Iran, saying he believed assurances from Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin that they were not yet doing so. Iran said it was in consultations with both countries. On his Truth Social network, the US president wrote: “Therefore, two major Countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them – Certainly not in their best interests.” Iran’s military said it had launched drone strikes on Friday morning against US military targets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait as it appeared there was no end in sight to the fighting. It told civilians across the region to stay 500 metres away from locations where US troops were present. The Houthis, who control northern and western Yemen, continued to claim a naval blockade on Saudi Arabian ports and ships using the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. The Houthis insisted on Friday that only Saudi-linked trade was under blockade as ships in the Red Sea broadcast messages to the group identifying ownership, flag and crew in the hope of securing a safe passage. The Houthis struck two Saudi tankers on Thursday in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, pushing oil prices up 7% to more than $100 per barrel for the first time since May. The attacks forced several other tankers to turn around and head north through the Suez canal, a much longer and more expensive route to reach Asia by sailing around ‌Africa. Shipping insurance costs through the southern Red Sea doubled for some companies on Thursday, sources said. Still, half of the 18 ships exiting Bab el-Mandeb on Thursday were carrying crude oil, including two Chinese supertankers. The number of tankers crossing through the strait of Hormuz fell to just one on Thursday, the lowest figure since 7 May. Trump wrote on social media that he would hold Iran accountable for any further Red Sea attacks, saying “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis themselves”. He told Axios he was considering relaunching major combat against Iran. “They haven’t received enough pain yet,” the US news outlet quoted Truump as saying. Washington and Tehran appear to remain fundamentally at odds over future control of the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, insisted the problem with advancing peace talks was “the American approach”. Araghchi said: “Preserving Iran’s interests in the strait of Hormuz is among our principles and we are committed to them. We are neither intimidated by threats nor will we yield to pressure. “As long as the legitimate goals and demands of the Iranian people are not met, it is natural that we continue our efforts.” Iranian officials had earlier suggested that the most recent US proposal involved a temporary arrangement that did not address control of the strait of Hormuz. Pakistan, which has acted as a mediator in the conflict, has also been pushing for fresh talks between the two sides after an initiative by ⁠China. Exploratory discussions took place during a visit by Iran’s interior minister, Eskandar Momeni, to Islamabad this week – his second within the last 10 days, sources said. Iranian state media said US missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz. Tehran said it had attacked US military equipment depots at Al-Adiri, officially named Camp Buehring, in northern Kuwait, and US troop positions at Camp Arifjan and Camp Doha near Kuwait City. It also said it had significantly damaged a surveillance tower used by the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain. In an example of how shipping disruption caused by the war affects other countries, ‌Coca-Cola has raised the prices of Diet Coke in India – where it is mainly sold in aluminium cans – by more than 10% as the conflict chokes its supply chain. Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Middle East crisis latest: US carries out strikes across Iran as Tehran targets American bases in region
summary: Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies
body: As we put the blog on pause for the time being, here is our full report on the latest attacks the US has launched against Iran and Donald Trump’s warning to Tehran: US missiles struck targets across Iran on Friday after Donald Trump vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the Middle East war to a second major shipping chokepoint, the mouth of the ⁠Red Sea. US Central Command said it targeted Iranian military command centres, communication networks, drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and maritime capabilities. Iranian armed forces responded by firing a wave of retaliatory attacks on at US bases in neighbouring Arab countries and warning people there that they may strike non-military buildings used by US personnel. The Iranian army said it used drones to target facilities in Bahrain and Jordan, with attacks also reported in Kuwait and Iraq. The IRGC warned civilians in the Middle East to stay away from US forces, state media reported. The head of Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya central military command, Ali Abdollahi, threatened US military personnel in the region on Friday, saying Iran had “prepared free, one-way tickets to hell for you”. “For every proud citizen of the Islamic Republic of Iran who is martyred, one American service member will be sent to hell,” he was quoted as saying by the state broadcaster. Iran pushed back on a New York Times (paywall) report from Thursday that Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire deal presented by the Iraqi prime minister, calling the report “completely diversionary and misleading,” according to state media IRNA. The NYT reported that the proposal was the only one on the table, and Tehran was not interested in a temporary deal which left the question of control of the strait of Hormuz unresolved, citing Iranian officials. Baghdad has also denied the NYT report. Trump said that in recent meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, both leaders assured the US president separately that they would not sell weapons to Iran. The US president added: “Two major countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them – certainly not in their best interests.” As we reported earlier, Iran’s military said on Friday that it carried out attacks targeting US military assets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait in retaliation for Washington’s latest strikes on the Islamic republic. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corp, meanwhile, said they had targeted a data centre in Bahrain belonging to Amazon, according to state media, though neither the US tech giant nor Bahrain have commented on the claim. There was also no confirmation from the US of any targeting of its facilities or personnel. “This morning, the fuel tanks, large equipment warehouses and silos, and the barracks of the US terrorist army forces at the Isa Air Base in Bahrain were targeted by Arash kamikaze drones,” the Iranian army said in a statement carried by state TV. An AFP journalist in Bahrain reported an explosion and warning sirens Friday, though it was not immediately clear if the two events were linked. Bahrain later said it intercepted and destroyed “a number of Iranian aerial aggressions”, accusing Tehran of targeting civilians. The Iranian army also claimed drone attacks against Jordan, targeting “aircraft hangars, aviation maintenance hangars and a barracks” at Al-Azraq base. Jordan’s military said it intercepted seven missiles and six drones launched by Iran on Friday, adding the operation “resulted in no casualties or material damage”. In a separate statement, the Iranian army said it had also launched drones at US equipment warehouses at Camp Udairi and the site of American military personnel at Camp Doha and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait. The IRGC said they had targeted the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, claiming to have destroyed an ammunition depot and inflicted casualties among US personnel. They also claimed attacks on equipment storage silos at Camp Udairi in Kuwait, as well as a US Fifth Fleet watchtower in Bahrain. The head of Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya central military command, Ali Abdollahi, threatened US military personnel in the region on Friday, saying Iran had “prepared free, one-way tickets to hell for you”. “For every proud citizen of the Islamic Republic of Iran who is martyred, one American service member will be sent to hell,” he was quoted as saying by the state broadcaster. Donald Trump said that in recent meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, both leaders assured the US president separately that they would not sell weapons to Iran. “Considering our relationship, I take him at his word,” Trump said of the Chinese leader. Meanwhile, the US president said that the Kremlin made the same guarantees, despite the ongoing war in Ukraine. Putin understands that the US does not sell weapons to Ukraine, “but to Nato countries”, Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Friday. “They pay full price, and how those weapons are distributed, I have no idea.” The US president added: “Two major countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them – certainly not in their best interests.” The US embassy in Amman has warned Americans that US military bases in Jordan should be avoided and asked Americans to follow local government and embassy travel advisories and guidance. It comes after three US service members were killed last week after Iran targeted a military base in Jordan. In a statement on X the embassy in the Jordanian capital added: “Due to heightened tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation. “US diplomatic facilities, including outside the Middle East, have been targeted. Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions.” It urged Americans to reconsider travelling to and through the Middle East, and to “exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions”. An Omani delegation has arrived in Iran to discuss a framework “to establish appropriate mechanisms for managing ship traffic in the strait of Hormuz,” Iranian state news agency IRNA reports. Tehran has maintained that it’s open to managing the strait in coordination with Oman, though the US and Gulf states have rejected the idea. Benjamin Netanyahu will meet Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister’s office said. “As part of the visit, the prime minister will meet with President Trump at the White House on Tuesday and attend the funeral service for Senator Lindsey Graham, a friend of Israel,” Netanyahu’s office said, adding that he will depart for Washington on Monday. Netanyahu’s visit comes at a time when tensions have mounted between the two leaders over the handling of the war with Iran and as Trump threatens to escalate US military action. Since Trump’s return to the White House last year, the two have already met six times, but this will be the first such meeting in five months. At the last one in February, Netanyahu made the case for the joint offensive against Iran that Trump launched with him weeks later. Iran has pushed back on a New York Times (paywall) report from Thursday that Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire deal presented by the Iraqi prime minister, calling the report “completely diversionary and misleading,” according to state media IRNA. The NYT reported that the proposal was the only one on the table, and Tehran was not interested in a temporary deal which left the question of control of the strait of Hormuz unresolved, citing Iranian officials. The IRNA report claimed the proposal was for a “temporary 10-day ceasefire”. Full details of the proposal have not been published. “Iran has always regarded diplomacy as having intrinsic value,” an unnamed Iranian official said, according to IRNA. “The problem of the escalation of conflict in the region stems exclusively from the United States’ breach of its promises and violation of the commitments contained in the June 18 memorandum of understanding.” Baghdad has also denied the NYT report. Ali al-Zaidi’s trip to Iran followed his recent visit to the White House where he met with Donald Trump. The Iraqi prime minister’s media office said the “claims” in the report were “completely baseless and had no connection to reality”, according to a statement published by the Iraqi News Agency (INA). The office urged media outlets “to verify information, rely on official sources and refrain from circulating unsubstantiated reports or claims attributed to anonymous sources”. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned civilians in the Middle East on Friday to stay away from US forces, state media reported. In an interview carried out by state TV, the IRGC said: We warn the general public in countries where American soldiers are stationed to immediately stay out of a radius of 500 metres from the places where American soldiers are hiding, in order to be safe. Jordan’s military said it intercepted seven missiles and six drones launched by Iran on Friday. The military said the interceptions, performed by air defence systems and air force planes, “resulted in no casualties or material damage,” according to AFP. Earlier on Friday, the Iranian army said it had launched drone attacks targeting US military personnel and military targets in Bahrain and Jordan after the US carried out its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran.
